connector: This is the last day of history before the novel begins. In the fall of 1943, the Nazis planned to take every Jewish person in Denmark. What happened next is one of the most remarkable stories of the whole war. Read it today, and you’ll be ready to meet Annemarie.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. This is the last history day before we open the novel. Today’s reading tells about October 1943, when the Nazis planned to arrest all the Jewish people in Denmark, and what ordinary Danes did about it. It’s a story about fear, and about courage. When you finish today, you’ll be ready for the book.
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is putting things side by side. You’ve read four short passages this week, and each one explains a little of the next. As you read today, look back at the other three. Ask how the occupation, the star law, and the king help explain what happened in October 1943.
transcripts.dol: Choose your sentence. Both are run together, with capitals missing. Today the model is about fishermen and the sea. Look at which words in it are names of peoples and countries. Then make your sentence into two clean sentences, each with a capital at the front and an end mark at the back.
transcripts.guide1: Today’s word work is review, with a twist. Some of what you see is already correct, and some isn’t. Your job is to tap only the mistakes. That means reading every item carefully, even the ones that look fine at first glance. Careful readers check before they change.
transcripts.morphology: Three spans are finished, and their lamps are lit. Today you lay the last four planks. When the final one is down, the bridge reaches the far shore, the shore of our new book. Read each meaning, choose the part that fits, and watch the bridge reach across.
transcripts.vocabulary: Today’s words come from the story of the rescue. Each one names a part of what happened: a warning, a plan, a secret journey. Read the sentence above each word, and picture the moment it describes. Then guess, and flip to check. You’ll meet ideas like these again in the novel.
transcripts.grammar: This is a draft with a few mistakes in it. Some sentences use the wrong form of a stand-in word, and some are already right. Read each one out loud. When something sounds off, try swapping in he, or him, to check. Tap only the sentences that need fixing.
transcripts.spelling: These words come from a draft, and some are misspelled. The mistakes are mostly in the middle of the word, where the vowels go soft and quiet. Say each word slowly, then picture how it really looks. Tap only the ones that are wrong, and leave the correct ones alone.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about remembering. Almost everyone in Denmark’s rescue story is gone now: the fishermen, the families, the king. One kind of courage is choosing not to forget them, and not to forget the people who were hurt. The author of our new book wrote it so that we would remember. Reading it is how you join in.
transcripts.read: Today’s passage has a warning, a time of hiding, and a journey across the sea. Watch for all the different kinds of people who helped. Not one hero, but many. When you reach the pause questions, think about what each person risked. And watch for the German man who sent the warning.
transcripts.guide3: Time for the week’s last writing. The first two questions are about the rescue itself. The third asks you to look back across all four readings, so think about the whole week, not just today. Then take your last step in this week’s writing project.
transcripts.chapter: The last question asks what made Denmark’s rescue so unusual. To answer it well, you need to compare. Think about what happened to Jewish people in other countries, and then what happened in Denmark. Name a specific fact from each side. A comparison is only as strong as its facts.
transcripts.workshop: Next week, you’ll write claims about Number the Stars. Today you practice choosing. Write a claim on two different topics, then ask which one you could give the most reasons for. The best claim isn’t always the one you feel most strongly about. It’s the one you have the most to say about.

a.raw: the danes saved over seven thousand people they sent them to sweden
a.fixed: The Danes saved over seven thousand people. They sent them to Sweden.
a.why: Capitals on The and Danes, a period after people, a capital T to start the second sentence, a capital on Sweden, and a period at the end.

b.raw: georg duckwitz warned the danish leaders word spread through copenhagen
b.why: Capitals on Georg Duckwitz, Danish and Copenhagen, a period after leaders, a capital W to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why the warning before October 1 mattered so much.
scholar.journal-q2: … and say which way you think took the most courage, and why.
scholar.journal-q3: … and use a fact from at least two different days this week.

match.occupation: Occupation is about one country taking control of another. Look for the meaning about taking over.
match.resistance: Resistance means pushing back. Look for the meaning about standing up against something wrong.
match.deport: Deport is about being sent out of a country. Look for the meaning about being forced to leave.
match.rescue: To rescue someone is to get them out of danger. Look for the meaning about saving.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Each right word lays a plank and the bridge reaches forward.

why.t: This week is a bridge between two books, from Anne’s island to Denmark, where Number the Stars takes place. trans- means across, so each word lays a plank across the water. pro- means forward, so the bridge reaches forward, one span each lesson, until it touches the far shore.

wordgame.win: The bridge reaches the far shore, and every lamp is lit. trans- = across, pro- = forward. Next week, the story begins.

notes.wgrd: Set several sources side by side. Each one explains part of another, and together they show the whole picture.
vocab: To stay alive through something dangerous.
To tell someone ahead of time that danger is coming.
When police or soldiers gather many people at once to take them away.
To move people or things secretly so others will not catch them.
When one country takes over and controls another.
Standing up against something you believe is wrong.
To force someone to leave a country, usually against their will.
notes.wordParts: trans- means “across” (transport, transmit). pro- means “forward” (protest, progress).
notes.grammar: Use the subject form to do the action and the object form to receive it. “Her went” should be “She went,” and “between you and I” should be “between you and me.”
notes.spelling: Watch the soft, unstressed middle of long words: mountain, campaign and certain all keep their ai even though you hardly hear it.
